t: What Even Is the Cloud?
hook: Cloud = electricity for computing. CapEx to OpEx.

lines.t: Coach, everyone says the cloud, but what is it actually?
Picture electricity. You don't build a power plant at home. You plug in and pay for what you use. The cloud is that, for computing.
So instead of buying my own servers, I rent them?
By the second. That's the big shift. From CapEx, buying equipment upfront, to OpEx, a monthly bill.
What's the payoff for a business?
Six advantages. Agility. Elasticity, scale up on Black Friday and down after. Global reach in minutes. And you stop guessing capacity.
Stop guessing capacity. I've seen that exact phrase in practice questions.
Because it's the signature line of cloud economics. If a question says stop guessing capacity, or pay as you go, the answer is the cloud, not on-premises.
So the one thing to remember is...
Cloud is electricity for computing. You flip a switch and pay the meter. CapEx becomes OpEx.
Before we go, quick recall. Don't peek. What's the cloud, in one line?

lines.prompt: What is the cloud, in one line?

lines.t: Electricity for computing. You flip a switch and pay the meter. CapEx becomes OpEx.
And the phrase that signals a cloud economics answer?
Stop guessing capacity. Pay as you go.

t: The Six Advantages of the Cloud
hook: Agility, elasticity, global, pay-as-you-go, stop guessing, economies of scale.

lines.t: The exam loves asking about cloud advantages. Give me the six in a way I'll never forget.
Think of a gym membership. Six perks. One, agility: try any class today. Two, elasticity: the gym adds treadmills in January and removes them in March.
Three?
Global reach: walk into any branch worldwide in minutes. Four, pay as you go: you pay for the days you actually show up.
Five and six?
Five, stop guessing capacity: the gym already knows how many treadmills you need. Six, economies of scale: because thousands of members share, the price per day is tiny.
So if a question lists one of those, the answer is cloud?
Right. Any one of the six is a cloud advantage. The exam often asks which is NOT an advantage, and the lie is usually fixed upfront cost, or managing your own data centers.
Memory hook?
Agility, elasticity, global, pay as you go, stop guessing, economies of scale. Six gym perks.
Recall. Which is NOT a cloud advantage?

lines.prompt: Which is NOT a cloud advantage?

lines.t: Fixed upfront cost, or managing your own data centers.
And the phrase for not overbuying hardware?
Stop guessing capacity.

t: Migration Strategies: The 7 Rs
hook: Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase, Retire, Retain, Revisit.

lines.t: Moving to the cloud has fancy names. The seven Rs. Help.
Picture moving house. Rehost is lift and shift, same stuff, new building. Replatform is a small renovation, like swapping the heating. Refactor is a full rebuild from scratch.
The other four?
Repurchase means drop and rebuy, like ditching your old CRM for a cloud one. Retire means throw it away, it's not needed. Retain means keep it on-premises for now. Revisit means decide later.
Exam tell for lift and shift?
Fastest, lowest risk, minimal change, that's Rehost. The phrase lift and shift is the giveaway.
And the one where you rebuild?
Refactor. Highest cost, highest long-term benefit. Cloud native.
Memory hook?
Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase, Retire, Retain, Revisit. Moving house, seven ways.
Recall. Fastest, lowest risk, minimal change?
Rehost, lift and shift.
Full rebuild, cloud native?
Refactor.

t: Sustainability & the Green Cloud
hook: Cloud is greener: AWS runs efficient data centers, you cut waste.

lines.t: There's a sustainability pillar now. What does the exam want?
Simple story. Your home server runs at full power all night, even when you sleep. AWS data centers share the load across thousands, so the lights are always efficiently used.
So moving to the cloud is greener?
Usually yes. You stop running underused hardware. The exam line is that cloud providers achieve higher utilization and lower carbon per workload.
Exam keyword?
Sustainability, carbon footprint, energy efficiency. The answer is almost always the cloud, or right-sizing, never over-provisioning.
Memory hook?
Shared data centers waste less power. Greener by sharing.
Recall. Why is the cloud greener?
Higher utilization, less wasted hardware and power.

t: IAM: The Bouncer and the Backstage Pass
hook: User = person. Role = temp pass for services. Policy = the rules.

lines.t: IAM confuses everyone. Users, roles, policies. Break it down.
Think of a concert venue. A User is a person with a long-term ID badge. A Role is a temporary backstage pass you hand to a service.
So a role is for machines, not people?
Exactly. An EC2 or a Lambda assumes a role to get temporary credentials. No passwords stored anywhere. That's least privilege in action.
And policies?
The rules printed on the pass. Which doors you can open. The golden rule is give the minimum, nothing more.
What's the exam trap?
If a question says no long-term credentials, or temporary access for a service, the answer is a Role, not a User.
Memory hook?
User is a person. Role is a temp pass for services. Policy is the rules on the pass.
Recall time. A service needs temporary access with no stored passwords. User or Role?

lines.prompt: Temporary access, no passwords: User or Role?

lines.t: Role. A temporary backstage pass for services.
And the golden rule of policies?
Least privilege. Give the minimum, nothing more.

t: Organizations & SCPs: The Family Rules
hook: Organizations = one family. SCP = house rules even parents follow.

lines.t: AWS Organizations and SCPs. How do they fit?
Organizations is one household with many rooms, each room an account. Consolidated billing is the single family electricity bill.
And SCPs?
House rules posted on the fridge. Even the parents, the admins, can't break them. An SCP can deny a region or a service across the whole family.
So an SCP can override an admin?
Yes. That's the key exam point. SCPs are guardrails that apply even to root and admins. They don't grant, they only limit.
Exam tell?
Multiple accounts, central governance, consolidated bill, that's Organizations. Prevent even admin, deny a region, that's an SCP.
Memory hook?
One family, one bill. House rules even parents follow.
Recall. Can an SCP block even an admin?

lines.prompt: Can an SCP block an admin?

lines.t: Yes. It's a guardrail that applies to everyone.
What gives one bill for many accounts?
Consolidated billing in Organizations.

t: KMS vs CloudHSM vs Secrets Manager
hook: KMS shared vault. CloudHSM your own vault. Secrets Manager rotating safe.

lines.t: Three key services that blur. KMS, CloudHSM, Secrets Manager.
KMS is a bank vault shared by many customers, managed by AWS. You use keys, AWS runs the building.
CloudHSM?
Your own private vault, single tenant, you run the hardware module. Needed for strict compliance like FIPS one hundred forty, level three.
Secrets Manager?
A safe that auto-rotates passwords. Database password, API key, it changes them on a schedule so they never go stale.
Exam tell for dedicated hardware?
Single tenant, dedicated HSM, FIPS level three, that's CloudHSM. Shared, managed, that's KMS.
Memory hook?
KMS shared vault, CloudHSM your vault, Secrets Manager rotating safe.
Recall. Dedicated single-tenant hardware module?
CloudHSM.
Auto-rotating database password?
Secrets Manager.

t: GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, WAF & Shield
hook: GuardDuty detective, Inspector building inspector, Macie PII, WAF bouncer, Shield umbrella.

lines.t: So many security tools. Give me one story each.
GuardDuty is a detective watching your logs for threats. Inspector is a building inspector scanning EC2 and containers for vulnerabilities.
Macie?
A metal detector for sensitive data, PII, in S3. Credit card, SSN, it finds them.
WAF and Shield?
WAF is a smart web bouncer, blocks SQL injection and cross site scripting at layer seven. Shield is an umbrella against DDoS, standard is free, advanced is paid.
Exam tell?
Threat detection in logs, GuardDuty. Vulnerability scan, Inspector. PII in S3, Macie. Web exploit, WAF. DDoS, Shield.
Memory hook?
Detective, inspector, metal detector, bouncer, umbrella.
Recall. PII hidden in S3?
Macie, the metal detector.
DDoS protection?
Shield, the umbrella.

t: CloudTrail vs CloudWatch vs Config
hook: CloudTrail who. CloudWatch how. Config what-state.

lines.t: These three sound identical. CloudTrail, CloudWatch, Config.
CloudTrail is CCTV. Who did what, and when. An API audit. Who deleted the bucket? CloudTrail.
CloudWatch?
The dashboard. Metrics and alarms. How is it performing? CPU spiking at 3am? That's CloudWatch.
And Config?
The inspector. What does my resource state look like, and did it drift from the rules? Compliance over time.
Give me the memory trick.
Trail is who. Watch is how. Config is what state. CCTV, dashboard, inspector.
So if the exam asks who made an API call...
CloudTrail. If it asks for a metric alarm, CloudWatch. If it asks about compliance drift, Config.
Recall. Who deleted the bucket? Which service?
CloudTrail, the CCTV.
CPU spiking at 3am, which service?
CloudWatch, the dashboard.

t: S3 vs EBS vs EFS: Warehouse, Locker, Shared Drive
hook: S3 object. EBS one server. EFS many servers.

lines.t: Three storage services, one blurry mess. S3, EBS, EFS.
S3 is a giant warehouse. Objects, accessed over the internet, basically unlimited, eleven nines of durability. Photos, backups, static websites.
And EBS?
A locker that plugs into one server in one data center. Fast block storage. It's your database's hard drive.
EFS?
A shared network drive that many servers mount at the same time. Perfect for lifting an old file share into the cloud.
How do I never mix them up again?
Say it as a story. Object storage is the warehouse, S3. One server is the locker, EBS. Many servers sharing files is the shared drive, EFS.
So if the question says shared file system across instances...
EFS. If it says object or static website, S3. If it says a single instance's volume, EBS.
Recall. Many servers sharing the same files?
EFS, the shared drive.
Object storage for a static website?

lines.prompt: Object storage for a static website?

lines.t: S3, the warehouse.

t: S3 Storage Classes: The Closet Scale
hook: Standard, IA, Glacier, Deep Archive = closet, attic, freezer, deep freeze.

lines.t: S3 has so many storage classes. Standard, IA, Glacier, Deep Archive.
Picture your home. Standard is the closet you use daily. Infrequent Access, IA, is the attic, cheaper to store but costs to fetch.
Glacier and Deep Archive?
Glacier is the freezer, minutes to hours to retrieve. Deep Archive is the deep freeze, cheapest, but takes up to twelve hours.
Exam tell for cheapest long term?
Cheapest, rarely accessed, long retention, that's Deep Archive. The phrase archive, or compliance retention, is the giveaway.
And frequent access with low latency?
Standard. The exam loves pairing Standard against IA when it says immediately available.
Memory hook?
Closet, attic, freezer, deep freeze. Standard, IA, Glacier, Deep Archive.
Recall. Cheapest, twelve hour retrieval?
Deep Archive, the deep freeze.
Daily use, immediate?
Standard, the closet.

t: RDS vs DynamoDB vs Aurora: The Restaurants
hook: RDS managed relational. DynamoDB key-value at any scale. Aurora MySQL turbo.

lines.t: Three databases. RDS, DynamoDB, Aurora. One story each.
RDS is a managed restaurant, you order relational, MySQL, Postgres, AWS cooks and cleans. You don't manage the kitchen.
DynamoDB?
A conveyor belt sushi bar. Key value, single digit millisecond, any scale. Perfect for shopping carts and leaderboards.
Aurora?
A turbocharged version of MySQL and Postgres. Up to five times faster, and it separates storage from compute so it scales automatically.
Exam tell for serverless, single digit millisecond?
DynamoDB. The phrases key value, any scale, or serverless, point there.
And for a managed relational engine?
RDS. If it says MySQL compatible but faster and auto scaling storage, that's Aurora.
Memory hook?
RDS managed restaurant, DynamoDB sushi belt, Aurora turbo MySQL.
Recall. Key value, any scale, single digit millisecond?
DynamoDB, the sushi belt.
MySQL compatible but faster, auto scaling?
Aurora, the turbo.

t: VPC & Security Groups vs NACLs: The Gated Community
hook: SG = per-house guard, stateful. NACL = community gate, stateless.

lines.t: VPC and all these acronyms. Where do I start?
A VPC is your gated community in the AWS neighborhood. You lay out the streets and decide who gets in.
Security Groups versus NACLs?
A Security Group is the guard at each house. Stateful, allow-only, and it follows the instance. A NACL is the community gate. Stateless, checks every car both directions, and it can allow or deny.
Stateful versus stateless, in plain words?
Stateful remembers the conversation, so reply traffic is auto-allowed. Stateless checks each direction separately.
Exam tell?
Instance-level and allow only, that's a Security Group. Subnet-level and can deny, that's a NACL.
Got it. Guard versus gate.
Guard versus gate. Say it once and it sticks.
Recall. Instance-level, allow only, stateful?
Security Group, the per-house guard.
Subnet-level, can deny, stateless?
NACL, the community gate.

t: Route 53, CloudFront & Global Accelerator
hook: Route53 GPS. CloudFront teleporter. Global Accelerator backbone.

lines.t: Three global services. Route 53, CloudFront, Global Accelerator.
Route 53 is GPS plus phonebook. It turns names into addresses, and it can route users to the nearest healthy copy.
CloudFront?
A teleporter for content. It caches your files at edge locations worldwide, so users get them from nearby, low latency.
Global Accelerator?
The AWS private motorway. It routes traffic over the AWS backbone, not the public internet, with static anycast IPs.
Exam tell for caching at the edge?
CDN, edge, low latency, that's CloudFront. DNS and routing policy, that's Route 53.
Memory hook?
GPS, teleporter, private motorway.
Recall. Caches content at edge locations?
CloudFront, the teleporter.
DNS and routing policies?
Route 53, the GPS.

t: Serverless & Containers: Food Truck vs Restaurant
hook: Lambda = food truck. Fargate = staffless restaurant.

lines.t: Lambda, Fargate, ECS, EKS. Too many kitchens.
Lambda is a food truck. You bring the code, it appears when an event rings the bell, runs up to fifteen minutes, then vanishes. No servers.
Fargate?
A restaurant where you don't manage the kitchen staff. You bring containers, AWS runs them. No servers to patch.
ECS versus EKS?
ECS is AWS's own restaurant brand. EKS is Kubernetes, the industry standard kitchen. Both can use Fargate to skip server management.
Least operational effort?
Lambda for short bursts. Fargate for containers. The phrase to circle is no server management.
Food truck and staffless restaurant.
That's the whole compute story in one line.
Recall. Short event-driven burst, no servers, max fifteen minutes?
Lambda, the food truck.
Containers, no server management?
Fargate, the staffless restaurant.

t: EC2 Auto Scaling & Load Balancing
hook: Auto Scaling adds lanes. ELB is the traffic officer.

lines.t: Auto Scaling and load balancing always appear together. Story?
Picture a theme park. Auto Scaling adds ride lanes when the queue grows, removes them when it shrinks. You set the target, like CPU at sixty percent.
And the load balancer?
The traffic officer directing guests to the shortest lane, and skipping any ride that's broken, health checks.
ALB versus NLB?
ALB is layer seven, it understands web traffic and paths. NLB is layer four, raw speed, millions of requests per second.
Exam tell?
Scale out automatically to meet demand, that's Auto Scaling. Distribute traffic and health check, that's ELB.
Memory hook?
Auto Scaling adds lanes. ELB is the traffic officer.
Recall. Distributes traffic, health checks?
Elastic Load Balancing.
Adds instances when demand rises?
Auto Scaling.

t: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge: The Post Office
hook: SQS queue. SNS broadcast. EventBridge router.

lines.t: SQS, SNS, EventBridge. Messaging soup.
SQS is a post office queue. One message, one worker pulls it, does the job. Decouples your app so spikes don't crash it.
SNS?
A broadcast tower. One message, many subscribers all get it. Email, SMS, Lambda, all at once.
EventBridge?
A smart mail sorter. It routes events from many sources to many targets based on rules. Like SaaS apps talking to AWS.
Exam tell for decoupling and buffering?
Queue, buffer, pull, that's SQS. Fan out, many subscribers, push, that's SNS.
Memory hook?
Queue, broadcast, router.
Recall. One message, many subscribers?
SNS, the broadcast.
Decouple with a buffer, workers pull?
SQS, the queue.

t: EC2 Pricing: Taxi, Season Pass, Carpool
hook: Taxi, season pass, carpool, prepaid card.

lines.t: On-Demand, Reserved, Spot, Savings Plans. Help me keep them straight.
On-Demand is a taxi. Pay per ride, no commitment. Reserved is a season pass. Commit one or three years, save up to seventy two percent.
Spot?
Carpool with strangers. Spare capacity, up to ninety percent off, but AWS can pull you over anytime. Great for fault-tolerant jobs.
And Savings Plans?
A prepaid transit card. You commit dollars per hour, but keep flexibility across instance families.
Exam keyword?
Most cost-effective and fault-tolerant, that's Spot. Steady, predictable, long term, that's Reserved or Savings Plans.
So four stories.
Taxi, season pass, carpool, prepaid card. Never mix them up again.
Recall. Cheapest, interruptible, fault-tolerant?
Spot, the carpool, up to ninety percent off.
Steady long-term commitment, biggest discount?
Reserved or Savings Plans, the season pass.

t: Billing Tools: Budgets, Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage
hook: Budgets alarm. Cost Explorer graphs. Cost and Usage Report raw data.

lines.t: Three billing tools. Budgets, Cost Explorer, Cost and Usage Report.
Budgets is a smoke alarm. Set a threshold, get alerted before you overspend. You can even set an S3 budget that stops a service.
Cost Explorer?
The dashboard with graphs. Visualize spend over time, filter by service, forecast the bill.
Cost and Usage Report?
The raw spreadsheet. The most detailed data, line by line, for deep analysis in a tool like Athena or QuickSight.
Exam tell for an alert before overspending?
Budgets. The phrase alert, or threshold, is the giveaway.
Memory hook?
Alarm, graphs, raw spreadsheet.
Recall. Get alerted before overspending?
AWS Budgets, the smoke alarm.
Most detailed line by line data?
Cost and Usage Report.

t: Support Plans: Basic to Enterprise
hook: Basic free. Developer business hours. Business 24/7. Enterprise TAM.

lines.t: Support plans confuse me. Basic, Developer, Business, Enterprise.
Basic is the free helmet, docs and community. Developer is business hours email support, for when you're testing.
Business and Enterprise?
Business is twenty four seven, phone and chat, for production. Enterprise adds a Technical Account Manager, a dedicated expert who knows your setup.
Exam tell for a dedicated expert?
TAM, that's Enterprise only. If the question says production, twenty four seven, that's Business at minimum.
Memory hook?
Helmet, email, twenty four seven, dedicated expert.
Recall. Which plan includes a TAM?
Enterprise.
Production, twenty four seven, phone and chat?
Business.

t: Well-Architected & Shared Responsibility
hook: AWS: security OF the cloud. You: security IN the cloud.

lines.t: The two big frameworks people fear. Well-Architected and Shared Responsibility.
Well-Architected is a health inspection with six pillars. Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability.
And Shared Responsibility?
Picture a restaurant. AWS owns the building, the ovens, the electricity. That's security of the cloud. You own the recipe, the ingredients, and your customers' safety. That's security in the cloud.
So who patches the operating system on EC2?
You do. That's your kitchen. But S3, RDS, Lambda, AWS handles the underlying infrastructure.
Exam line?
Physical or AWS-managed infrastructure, that's AWS. Data, IAM, configuration, that's you. That split is two or three free marks.
Security of versus security in.
Of the cloud is AWS. In the cloud is you. Nail that and you've nailed a whole domain.
Recall. Who patches the operating system on EC2?

lines.prompt: Who patches the EC2 operating system?

lines.t: You do. That's security in the cloud.
Who owns the physical data centers?
AWS. Security of the cloud.

t: Disaster Recovery: The Four Patterns
hook: Backup, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Site = spare tire, idling engine, warm engine, twin car.

lines.t: Disaster recovery has four patterns. Make them stick.
Backup and restore is a spare tire in the trunk. Slow to swap, cheapest. Pilot light is an idling engine, minimal always on, scale up fast.
Warm standby and multi-site?
Warm standby is a warm engine, scaled down but ready, seconds to failover. Multi-site is a twin car, fully running, active active, near zero downtime, most expensive.
Exam tell for cheapest?
Backup and restore. Lowest cost, longest recovery. The exam pairs cost against recovery time.
And near zero downtime?
Multi-site, active active. Most expensive, highest availability.
Memory hook?
Spare tire, idling engine, warm engine, twin car.
Recall. Cheapest, longest recovery?
Backup and restore, the spare tire.
Near zero downtime, active active?
Multi-site, the twin car.
